Six things 23 years in the classroom taught me about leadership

Early in her teaching career, Dr Katie Trowbridge discovered that real leadership happens when you are open to pushback. Now she lives by the CREATE Method, with curiosity, risk, experience, attitude, teamwork and evaluation translating directly from the classroom to leadership.
  • By Katie Trowbridge
  • Tags: Education, Leadership, Skills
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:41
Instaread

Early in my teaching career, I believed my job was to have the answers. Every lesson was planned to the minute, and I walked into class each day confident I knew exactly where it was going. Sometimes it went beautifully. Sometimes the students had other plans.

Jesse, a junior in my American Literature class, taught me one of my most valuable leadership lessons. I had just introduced an exciting new unit when he walked up to me after class, blank paper in hand, and said: “I’m not doing this assignment. I just don’t see the purpose”. Ouch.

That night at home, after getting over my initial reaction of “How rude”, I decided to ask Jesse more questions. What made this assignment lack purpose? How might you create one that has meaning and still fits within the required curriculum? 

With Jesse’s help, we co-created a unit the entire class embraced. I learned that real leadership happens when you are open to pushback.

Over the years, lessons like that one settled into six habits I now call the CREATE Method: curiosity, risk, experience, attitude, teamwork and evaluation. Each one translates directly from the classroom to leadership.

Too often, leaders feel pressure to be the person with the right answer. That mindset can unintentionally teach people to wait for direction and stay silent. Great teachers and great leaders do something different: they develop people who own their own thinking.

1. Curiosity comes before compliance

We often mistake a quiet classroom for an engaged one. Students can complete every assignment, follow every instruction and still be intellectually absent.

In a national survey of 1,000 employed US adults that we conducted with The Center for Generational Kinetics, two factors stood out as barriers to deeper thinking: fear and mental fatigue. 

People attend meetings, complete tasks and meet deadlines without feeling curious about what they are doing or why it matters. Fear of judgement keeps them from asking the questions they need answered, and mental overload means many simply opt out of their own thinking.

Curiosity begins when leaders replace some of their answers with better questions. Instead of: “Does everyone understand?”, try: “What are we overlooking?” or: “What doesn’t make sense yet?”. And when an employee challenges you, pause before responding. Instead of: “That’s how we’ve always done it”, ask: “What have you noticed?”. That small shift communicates that their thinking matters.

Too often, leaders feel pressure to be the person with the right answer. That mindset can unintentionally teach people to wait for direction and stay silent

2. Risk requires emotional safety

Students rarely share an unconventional idea when they believe getting it wrong will make them look foolish. Adults are no different. Our survey showed that feeling valued, heard and seen is a top concern for employees.

Telling students to take risks was never enough. I had to show them what happened when my own idea failed or a first attempt fell short. Leaders create the same conditions through their everyday reactions. Do you become impatient when someone struggles? Do you dismiss an unfinished idea?

Encouraging thoughtful risk does not mean lowering standards. It means separating an unsuccessful attempt from the person who made it. Ask: “What did this teach us?” before: “What went wrong?”

3. Experience is a source of insight

No two students walked into my classroom with the same view of the world. Dustin loved to rock the boat. If there was an opposite side to an argument, he would take it. 

When I treated his challenges as distractions, learning narrowed and Dustin shut down. When I treated them as resources, everyone’s thinking expanded, including mine.

Workplaces are full of people whose experience lets them see risks and opportunities others miss. Yet leaders often seek input only after they have already framed the challenge and chosen a likely solution.

Invite people into the thinking earlier. Ask who has experienced the issue most directly, whose work will be affected and whose perspective is missing. 

Then listen without defending the current approach. The people closest to a challenge often hold insight that those with the most authority do not.

Encouraging thoughtful risk does not mean lowering standards. It means separating an unsuccessful attempt from the person who made it

4. Attitude shapes possibility

Every classroom has its version of “This will never work”. So does every meeting.

Just as I learned from Jesse, resistance is not always negativity. It can signal fear, fatigue, previous disappointment or knowledge that has not yet been heard. 

My job was never to silence resistance but to understand what sat underneath it and help students see where they still had agency.

Leaders can do the same by turning: “No, because…” into: “What would need to be true?”. That question doesn’t force false optimism.

5. Teamwork is more than putting people together

I could walk past any group in my classroom and tell you within 10 seconds who was running it, who was doing the work and who had quietly checked out. The project got finished. The thinking didn’t. Somewhere along the way I had confused sitting together with working together.

Meetings do the same thing. So before a project starts, ask each person what they bring to it. Decide together how decisions get made and what happens when you disagree. And watch yourself: if your voice is always first, it is probably also the loudest.

Build reflection in while it still counts: What is working? What needs to change? What will we try next?

6. Evaluation should guide growth, not just judge performance

Every teacher knows the look. You hand back an essay you spent time marking and the student flips straight to the grade, throws it into the recycling bin and never reads a word. 

Why would they? The work is over. The feedback that improved anything were the ones I gave while they were still writing.

Annual reviews work the same way. They arrive after the work they judge is finished. 

Build reflection in while it still counts: What is working? What needs to change? What will we try next? Evaluation is information, not a verdict.

Stop proving and start developing

The classroom taught me that leadership is not about proving how much you know. It is about developing the capacity of the people around you.

Choose one conversation this week in which you would normally provide the answer. Pause. Ask one more question. Give someone space to struggle productively before stepping in.

Great teachers prepare students to leave the classroom with the curiosity, courage and judgement to think for themselves. Great leaders should aim to do the same.
